topics: Batch sizing and latency vs cost
transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-08-13 15:00 UTC, duration ~62 min. Attendees: John Carter (Redwood AE), Maya Singh (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (Redwood SE), Elena Park (CTO, Novara), Raj Patel (ML Eng), Samir Joshi (PM), Priya Mehta (SRE).

Summary: quick recap of current Novara stack: self-hosted model currently on k8s with Triton, looking to reduce per-request token cost and hit 95th %-ile latency SLAs. Interested in Redwood Optimize console to generate prefetch+batch recommendations and run an economic simulation.

00:00:08 John Carter: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, um, quick intro from our side — Maya and Lena from SE. Um, Elena, do you want to open with what you're hoping to get out of this session?
00:00:22 Elena Park: Sure, yeah thanks John. Uh, high level — we're doing a rollout for 3rd party summarization and chat and the costs have been spiking. We need to hit a cost target while keeping p95 under about 120 milliseconds. Stakeholders are finance + infra.
00:00:40 Raj Patel: And the workload is bursty — most requests short, 1-2 turns, but some long sessions for power users. We also have a session store today but it's not keyed for prefix reuse.
00:00:55 Maya Singh: Great, that's the exact pattern where prefix/KV prefetch helps. Quick agenda: demo Optimize console cost-sim, show batching profiles, then recommend TTLs and prefetch heuristics, and end with next steps.

00:01:12 Lena Ortiz: One note — we'll use your sample trace that Raj uploaded, and then show simulated runs across three modes: hosted, reserved/dedicated, and hosted-with-prefetch.

00:03:05 Maya Singh: Opening the console — this is the Optimize tab, we have a workload simulator. Please excuse the auto-caption, sometimes it calls our product Redwood Optima in the transcript.
00:03:18 (laughter)

00:03:30 Maya Singh: Alright, first chart is request distribution, your histogram shows 72% of requests < 50 tokens, 18% between 50-250, and tail beyond that. That suggests small-batch opportunities.
00:03:52 Raj Patel: That matches our figures. The problem we saw is the cold KV miss for returning sessions, we re-run a bunch of prompt prefixes every time.
00:04:06 Maya Singh: Exactly. With prefix caching we get two levers: cache hit rate (depends on session affinity + TTL) and prefetching early in session to warm KV. Prefetch can be scheduled when we see session start or at Nth token.

00:05:20 John Carter: Walk us through the cost model — what assumptions is the console using?
00:05:28 Maya Singh: Good question. The simulator combines token compute cost (per-vram-second normalized), amortized GPU instance cost for reserved capacity, and an estimate for KV store egress/storage. We parametrize request concurrency, average sequence length, and batch window. The output is per-1M-requests unit cost.
00:05:48 Elena Park: The KV store cost — is that per-lookup or per-Gb? For us network egress inside cloud is significant.
00:05:58 Maya Singh: We model both: a per-lookup small cost and a storage GB/mo. For on-prem customers we can zero out egress. The console shows breakdown by compute vs KV vs idle (reserved) cost.

00:07:10 Lena Ortiz: Now toggling prefetch — we simulate two modes: lookahead prefetch (fetch likely next KV pages) and session-prefetch (on session start fetch prefix tokens). Lookahead is cheaper if your sessions have predictable patterns.
00:07:35 Samir Joshi: In our UX, we know the user intent after the first message about 60% of the time. Could that drive more aggressive prefetch?
00:07:44 Maya Singh: Yes — you can use a classifier signal to gate prefetch. The console supports a 'prefetch probability' param so you can simulate imperfect predictions.

00:09:02 Maya Singh: Ok here's a scenario: baseline hosted (no prefetch, batch window 5ms) yields per-1M cost: $X (compute dominant) and p95 latency 85ms. If we add prefix prefetch with 10s TTL and a conservative 40% hit rate, cost reduces by ~21% but p95 jumps marginally to 92ms due to extra prefetch overhead.
00:09:35 Raj Patel: Wait can we get numbers relative to reserved capacity? Our CFO prefers committing if the unit cost drops significantly.
00:09:44 Maya Singh: Yes. In reserved mode (2x reserved pods sized for 500 qps) the amortized idle cost is higher but variable token cost lower. With optimal batching (batch window increased to 20ms for small requests), we see another ~15% savings but p95 may climb if traffic is very spiky.

00:11:00 Elena Park: What about TTLs — 10s seems short. Our sessions can be reused across minutes.
00:11:08 Maya Singh: TTL is a knob. We typically pick 10-60s based on session revisit rate and memory budget. Longer TTL increases hit rate but costs more in KV storage and memory. In the console we show hit rate vs memory footprint tradeoff.

00:12:05 Priya Mehta: For SRE concerns: does prefetch increase peak QPS? If we prefetch for many sessions simultaneously we might spike load.
00:12:15 Lena Ortiz: Good point. Prefetch should be throttled and staggered; console includes a prefetch concurrency cap. We recommend ramping prefetch across hosts and using jitter to smooth spikes.

00:13:30 John Carter: Can we walk through a concrete recommendation for Novara's sample trace?
00:13:36 Maya Singh: Sure — based on your histogram and session revisit rate, recommended starting config: batch window 12ms, session TTL 45s, prefetch probability 0.6 gated by intent classifier, prefetch concurrency cap 200, KV LRU size 8GB per shard. That yields simulated savings ~28% vs baseline hosted no-prefetch and keeps p95 under 120ms in 95% of simulated days.
00:14:10 Raj Patel: That LRU size seems large. What's the memory impact on our nodes?
00:14:17 Maya Singh: It's a per-shard cache; depends on shard count. The console will show aggregated memory and per-GPU additional memory usage. We also have quantized KV representations to reduce footprint.

00:16:05 Samir Joshi: If we go dedicated reserved, do we need to change the prefetch heuristics?
00:16:12 Maya Singh: Yes — reserved capacity allows more aggressive batching since throughput is predictable. You can increase batch window to 25-30ms and push TTLs longer because idle costs are amortized. But watch latency SLOs.

00:17:20 Raj Patel: We saw some other vendors recommend aggressive batching which increased median latency but saved cost. Our product team cares about both. How do you pick sweet spot?
00:17:30 Maya Singh: The console has an optimization slider — you pick a weighting between cost vs latency and it proposes configurations. For example, set cost weight 0.7 and latency weight 0.3 and it outputs batch window 18ms, TTL 35s, estimated 23% savings.

00:19:05 Elena Park: Security — our compliance needs audit logs for KV access and encryption for keys. How does Redwood handle KMS and audit?
00:19:14 John Carter: We support customer-managed KMS/HSM integrations in Private, and encryption-in-transit for hosted. There are audit logs available in Redwood Console with per-request trace IDs. We can schedule a security deep-dive.
00:19:38 Priya Mehta: Also SSO — SAML?
00:19:41 John Carter: Yes, SAML and OIDC supported. We'll include the security pack in the follow-up.

00:20:45 Maya Singh: Back to the console: I'm toggling a sensitivity analysis now — here's worst-case day (spiky traffic): prefetch unbounded causes 9% higher peak compute, but with a concurrency cap you can eliminate that spike while keeping 18% of the savings.
00:21:18 Raj Patel: Can we see the per-token cost breakdown?
00:21:22 Maya Singh: Yes, compute is 68%, KV lookup 6%, idle/reserved 26% in your baseline. With prefetch+batch we push compute down to 52% and idle slightly up — the sim shows redistributed cost.

00:23:05 Lena Ortiz: There's also an option to selectively prefetch for 'heavy' users only, i.e., if user has >X historical tokens. That gives high hit rate with lower total prefetch volume.
00:23:22 Samir Joshi: That might map well to our power user cohort.

00:25:00 Maya Singh: Quick demo of runbook: console can export recommended config as a JSON policy for the runtime — batch window, TTLs, prefetch rules, and fallbacks. We also show a canary rollout plan.
00:25:20 Raj Patel: Good — we prefer canary first on 10% traffic.

00:27:05 Maya Singh: Now a note on model routing: if we fallback to smaller quantized model when latency climbs, you get graceful degradation. Console will simulate mixing models and show overall quality/cost tradeoffs.
00:27:28 Elena Park: Hmm does Redwood support model-level A/B? We need to test quality regressions.
00:27:34 Maya Singh: Yes, rollouts/A-B per route, and you can tie quality alerts to your prompt test suite.

00:29:12 Priya Mehta: For the benchmark you mentioned — what sample data should we provide?
00:29:18 Maya Singh: Ideal: 24 hours of anonymized request traces with timestamps, session ids, token counts, and the decision signals (if any). The simulator needs distribution to model temporal correlation. Raj, you said you can provide histograms?
00:29:32 Raj Patel: I can extract that today and add the raw 6h sample.

00:31:50 John Carter: Let's cover edge cases: a) burst startup where many sessions are created simultaneously b) long lived sessions with huge caches c) adversarial users with many unique prefixes
00:32:05 Lena Ortiz: For (a) stagger prefetch and use jitter. For (b) cap KV LRU or use a tiered eviction. For (c) reduce prefetch probability for unknown users and rely on on-demand cache fill.

00:33:44 Samir Joshi: Any integration work for our infra? Right now Triton + in-house KV.
00:33:52 Maya Singh: Integration points are the runtime SDK (open-source client), a KV adapter (Redis-compatible or S3-backed), and a small sidecar for prefetch orchestration. We can provide the adapters and reference Helm chart.
00:34:25 Raj Patel: Will there be a penalty if we keep our KV on-prem while runtime is hosted?
00:34:33 Lena Ortiz: Network latency matters. For hosted runtime, colocating KV or using a proxied cache is recommended. The console can simulate added network latency.

00:36:10 Maya Singh: Ok running a quick sim: baseline per-1M requests $1,024 (hypothetical), with the recommended config we show $738 — ~28% savings. Tail p95 stays 92ms. If we move to reserved with bigger batch we get $610 but p95 in worst-case days can rise to ~140ms unless we constrain batch windows.
00:36:48 Elena Park: So reserved only when we're comfortable with traffic predictability. Finance will want the absolute $ numbers vs percent.
00:36:58 John Carter: We'll include both dollar numbers and sensitivity bands in the sheet.

00:38:30 Maya Singh: A few practical tips: 1) Start with conservative TTL (30-45s) 2) Use classifier gating for prefetch to control volume 3) Set prefetch concurrency cap and jitter 4) Canary rollout at 10% then 50% before full.
00:38:52 Raj Patel: For the classifier gating, is that something Redwood provides or we bring our own?
00:38:58 Maya Singh: It's flexible — you can use your own model or Redwood can host a lightweight intent classifier as part of the routing layer. We recommend evaluating your classifier precision first.

00:40:10 Priya Mehta: On observability — do we get token-level tracing and cost attribution per route?
00:40:17 John Carter: Yes, Console gives token-level cost breakdowns per route and per model — you can filter by customer tenant or API key.

00:42:05 Samir Joshi: Ok last section — can we run the short benchmark and then reconvene to finalize runbook?
00:42:14 John Carter: Absolutely. Proposed plan: Raj provides sample trace by 2025-08-16, Maya runs 24h sim/benchmark week of 8/18, then we do a results review on 8/22 with security in parallel.
00:42:32 Elena Park: Works for us.

00:43:00 (crosstalk, small talk)
00:44:15 John Carter: Quick Q & A — Samir: about pricing tiers — we have per-token hosted pricing and reserved capacity discounts; we'll include an apples-to-apples sheet.
00:44:40 Samir Joshi: Good. Also curious if our customers in EU require data residency — we might need a private deployment in region.
00:44:49 John Carter: We support private deployments and region pinning. We'll flag that to the product team for design.

00:46:10 Maya Singh: Closing notes: expect the sandbox invite and cost-sim spreadsheet by Friday 2025-08-15. We'll also include the runbook export and the recommended starting config.
00:46:28 Raj Patel: One last thing — any guides for TTL heuristics? A blog or playbook?
00:46:34 Lena Ortiz: Yes, we'll send the prefetch playbook and an example Helm chart.

00:47:50 Elena Park: Thanks all, that was helpful.
00:48:00 John Carter: Thanks — we'll follow up with the artifacts.
00:48:05 (meeting ends)

Artifacts referenced: cost-sim spreadsheet (link: /redwood/sim/novara-costsim-0813), prefetch playbook doc (link: /docs/prefetch-playbook), Helm chart repo (link: github.com/redwood-inference/prefetch-helm).

Notes on transcript quality: speaker labels occasionally generic; some product names mis-transcribed (Redwood Optimize -> Redwood Optima) but content preserved.
